title: Microwave-driven same-species sympathetic cooling for trapped ions
authors: M. C. Smith, E. Vandrey, A. D. Leu, N. Drotleff, A. Agrawal, K. Miyanishi, D. M. Lucas, M. F. Gely
abstract: Sympathetic cooling of data qubits by coolant ions is an essential technique for trapped-ion quantum computing. Conventionally a second ion species is used, requiring additional lasers and complicating optical setups. We propose a scheme for sympathetic cooling using the same species and test it for $^{43}$Ca$^+$ ions. Pulsed sideband cooling and ion addressing are implemented via integrated microwave control, further simplifying optical requirements. We cool a two-ion gate mode close to its ground state ($\bar{n}\approx 0.16$) and benchmark an induced error on the data qubit of $1.7(4)\times 10^{-4}$ per cooling cycle.
summary: The paper introduces a microwave-driven scheme to sympathetically cool trapped ions using only ions of the same species, eliminating complex optical setups. They successfully cooled $	ext{}^{43}	ext{Ca}^+$ ions close to their motional ground state while simultaneously measuring low error rates on the data qubit. This advancement simplifies the hardware requirements for scalable quantum computation.
main_problem: To develop a sympathetic cooling technique for trapped ions that uses only ions of the same species, thereby simplifying complex optical setups required by conventional methods.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated near-ground-state cooling ($ ar{n} \approx 0.16$) using microwave-driven sideband cooling on $	ext{}^{43}	ext{Ca}^+$ ions with an induced error of $1.7(4) 	imes 10^{-4}$ per cycle.
method: The scheme employs pulsed sideband cooling driven by global microwave fields, which is combined with interleaved randomized benchmarking (IRB) to quantify the resulting error on the data qubit.
model_or_system: The physical system is a trapped ion crystal of $	ext{}^{43}	ext{Ca}^+$ ions confined in a surface-electrode Paul trap. Cooling occurs via microwave driving of the coolant ion's motional sideband, while quantum operations are performed on the data qubit within its electronic ground state manifold.
key_observables: Average phonon occupation ($ ar{n}$), induced error rate per cooling cycle ($1.7(4) 	imes 10^{-4}$), and cooling rate (e.g., $0.27$ quanta/cycle).
important_parameters: The minimum achievable phonon occupation ($ ar{n} \approx 0.16$), the error per cycle, and the frequency shifts induced by microwave pulses.
main_assumptions: The method assumes the availability of multiple states within the ground manifold for general applicability beyond $	ext{}^{43}	ext{Ca}^+$. The measured errors are dominated by technical sources like MW drive chain thermal drifts.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the cooling scheme using Zeeman splittings, show exponential decay of phonon occupation ($ ar{n}$) over cycles, and detail the interleaved randomized benchmarking protocol used to measure data qubit error.
paper_structure: The paper details the microwave-driven sympathetic cooling mechanism, presents measurements confirming near-ground-state cooling efficiency, and rigorously quantifies the resulting decoherence/error on the quantum data qubit using advanced error mitigation techniques like spin-echo pulses.
why_interesting: This work represents a significant engineering advance in trapped-ion quantum computing by simplifying the required laser infrastructure while maintaining high fidelity for both cooling and computation.

FIG. 1. Same-isotope sympathetic cooling scheme. (a) Data ions and coolant ions are trapped within the same potential well, leading to shared motional modes. Coolant ions are used to cool the shared motion of all ions without affecting the information stored in the electronic states of the data ions. Errors in quantum logic operations between data ions, which make use of this shared motion, are thus reduced. A surface-electrode Paul trap is used to confine the two ions 40 µm above the trap surface and an integrated microwave waveguide is used to generate a magnetic field for driving pulsed sideband cooling, individual ion addressing, and quan- tum logic operations (ions not to scale).
